newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Europe urges ASEAN to put pressure on Burma.
newsitem.headline: Europe urges ASEAN to put pressure on Burma.

text.p: The European Union (EU) said on Friday it had urged Southeast Asian nations to pressure Burma in whatever way it chooses in an effort to reform a regime widely accused of human rights abuses.

A robust exchange on how to deal with the military rulers in Burma and other human rights issues dominated two days of talks between the 15-member EU and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

"In Europe, we feel what is happening in Burma is absolutely unacceptable in terms of violations of human rights," Dutch Foreign Minister and current EU President Hans Van Mierlo said during a news conference.
Different cultures dictate different approaches on how to deal with a regime that has brutally cracked down on the pro-democracy movement led by Nobel Peace Prize-winner Aung San Suu Kyi, he said.
"But the main thing for everybody is that we have to fight it wherever violations of human rights are, whether it is in Africa, Asia or Europe," he said at the end of the meetings.
"The main message of Europe was, 'please, do what you can do in your region to influence the affairs. The way you do it, that is not for us to dictate... But we count on you to do it.'"
Burma is due to join ASEAN -- which currently groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- possibly as early as this year.
That has prompted closed-door talks on how the EU will deal with an ASEAN that includes a regime it is trying to ostracize.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told a news conference that his country would not, for the moment at least, lift its refusal to give visas to senior Burmese officials.
"The attitude of France will not change for the moment."
Asian ministers were clearly not pleased by such talk.

"They (EU) are in fact suggesting that ASEAN delay admission of Myanmar (Burma) because they will have difficulty dealing with Myanmar unless there are some basic changes in the fundamental law of the land," Philippines Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon told reporters.
"We say that's our business," Siazon declared.
Conference co-chairman, Singapore Foreign Minister Shanmugam Jayakumar, said the two-hour discussion on Burma was the most substantive in the 20-year history of ASEAN-EU meetings.
Jayakumar quoted one ASEAN minister, whom he did not identify, as saying EU demands that ASEAN get tough with Burma as a condition of membership was like a pre-nuptial agreement.

"He put it this way. The EU would like ASEAN to negotiate a pre-nuptial agreement with Myanmar (Burma). But he said ASEAN's response is that in Asia, we marry first but expect the bride to adapt her behaviour to the marriage."
ASEAN calls its approach "constructive engagement".

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said on Wednesday that political repression and human rights violations in Burma last year reached their highest levels since the suppression of a popular uprising at the end of the 1980s.
An Amnesty report called on ASEAN to end its "constructive engagement" with Rangoon.
Indonesian President Suharto will visit Burma next week, the first senior statesman to visit the country in several years.
State Secretary Moerdiono said on Thursday Suharto would make a week-long visit to Burma, Cambodia and Laos starting February 19.

Moerdiono said the visit had nothing to do with Burma's pending membership in ASEAN. He said Suharto would witness an agreement between Citra Lamtoro Gung, a firm controlled by his eldest daughter, and the Union of Myanmar Economic Holding.
Suharto last visited Burma in 1974.
